question:
Solve for $x$:
$$x + 3\sqrt{x + 2} = 2$$
memo:
$$x + 3\sqrt{x + 2} = 2$$
$$3\sqrt{x + 2} = 2 - x$$
$$\left(3\sqrt{x + 2}\right)^2 = (2 - x)^2$$
$$9(x + 2) = 4 - 4x + x^2$$
$$9x + 18 = x^2 - 4x + 4$$
$$x^2 - 13x - 14 = 0$$
$$(x - 14)(x + 1) = 0$$
$$x = 14 \quad \text{or} \quad x = -1$$
$$\text{Check } x = 14: \quad 14 + 3\sqrt{14 + 2} = 14 + 12 = 26 \ne 2 \implies x \ne 14$$
$$\text{Check } x = -1: \quad -1 + 3\sqrt{-1 + 2} = -1 + 3(1) = 2 \implies x = -1$$
$$\therefore x = -1$$

* $\checkmark$ isolating the surd
* $\checkmark$ squaring both sides (method)
* $\checkmark$ standard form
* $\checkmark$ answer with selection ($x = -1$)

question: A rectangle having sides of $(y - 3)\text{ metres}$ and $(x + 2)\text{ metres}$ has a perimeter of $24\text{ metres}$ and an area of $32\text{ square metres}$. Calculate the values of $x$ and $y$.
memo:
$$\text{Area: } (y - 3)(x + 2) = 32$$
$$yx + 2y - 3x - 6 = 32 \quad \dots (1)$$

$$\text{Perimeter: } 2(y - 3) + 2(x + 2) = 24$$
$$2y - 6 + 2x + 4 = 24$$
$$2y + 2x - 2 = 24$$
$$y + x - 1 = 12$$
$$y = 13 - x \quad \dots (2)$$

$$\text{Substitute (2) into (1):}$$
$$(13 - x - 3)(x + 2) = 32$$
$$(10 - x)(x + 2) = 32$$
$$10x + 20 - x^2 - 2x = 32$$
$$-x^2 + 8x - 12 = 0$$
$$x^2 - 8x + 12 = 0$$
$$(x - 6)(x - 2) = 0$$
$$x = 6 \quad \text{or} \quad x = 2$$

$$\text{If } x = 6: \quad y = 13 - 6 = 7$$
$$\text{If } x = 2: \quad y = 13 - 2 = 11$$

$$\mathbf{OR/OF}$$

$$\text{From perimeter: } x = 13 - y \quad \dots (2)$$
$$\text{Substitute into area:}$$
$$(y - 3)(13 - y + 2) = 32$$
$$(y - 3)(15 - y) = 32$$
$$15y - y^2 - 45 + 3y = 32$$
$$-y^2 + 18y - 77 = 0$$
$$y^2 - 18y + 77 = 0$$
$$(y - 7)(y - 11) = 0$$
$$y = 7 \quad \text{or} \quad y = 11$$
$$\text{If } y = 7: \quad x = 13 - 7 = 6$$
$$\text{If } y = 11: \quad x = 13 - 11 = 2$$

* $\checkmark$ setting up eq 1 (Area)
* $\checkmark$ setting up eq 2 (Perimeter)
* $\checkmark$ substitution
* $\checkmark$ standard form
* $\checkmark$ $x$-values
* $\checkmark$ $y$-values

question: Show that $(1 + x^m + x^{-n})^2 - (1 - x^m - x^{-n})^2$ is divisible by $2$ for all real values of $m$ and $n$.
memo:
$$(1 + x^m + x^{-n})^2 - (1 - x^m - x^{-n})^2$$
$$= \left[(1 + x^m + x^{-n}) - (1 - x^m - x^{-n})\right] \left[(1 + x^m + x^{-n}) + (1 - x^m - x^{-n})\right]$$
$$= [1 + x^m + x^{-n} - 1 + x^m + x^{-n}] [1 + x^m + x^{-n} + 1 - x^m - x^{-n}]$$
$$= [2(x^m + x^{-n})][2]$$
$$= 4(x^m + x^{-n}) = 2\left[2(x^m + x^{-n})\right]$$
$$\text{Since } 2\left[2(x^m + x^{-n})\right] \text{ has a factor of } 2, \text{ it is divisible by } 2 \text{ for all real values of } m \text{ and } n.$$

$$\mathbf{OR/OF}$$

$$\text{Expanding both squares:}$$
$$(1 + x^m + x^{-n})^2 = 1 + 2x^m + 2x^{-n} + x^{2m} + 2x^{m-n} + x^{-2n}$$
$$(1 - x^m - x^{-n})^2 = 1 - 2x^m - 2x^{-n} + x^{2m} + 2x^{m-n} + x^{-2n}$$
$$\text{Subtracting:}$$
$$(1 + x^m + x^{-n})^2 - (1 - x^m - x^{-n})^2 = 4x^m + 4x^{-n} = 4(x^m + x^{-n}) = 2\left[2(x^m + x^{-n})\right]$$
$$\therefore \text{divisible by } 2.$$

* $\checkmark$ factorisation / expansion
* $\checkmark$ 2 (or 4)
* $\checkmark 2\left[2(x^m + x^{-n})\right]$ (or $4(x^m + x^{-n})$)

question: Consider the first $21$ terms of the sequence $T_n = 2^{n+2}$. Calculate the sum of the terms in this sequence that are not powers of $4$.
memo:
$$\text{Terms of the sequence: } T_n = 2^{n+2}$$
$$T_1 = 2^3 = 8 \quad (\text{not a power of } 4)$$
$$T_2 = 2^4 = 16 = 4^2 \quad (\text{power of } 4)$$
$$T_3 = 2^5 = 32 \quad (\text{not a power of } 4)$$
$$T_4 = 2^6 = 64 = 4^3 \quad (\text{power of } 4)$$

$$\text{The terms that are not powers of } 4 \text{ are the odd-numbered terms: } T_1, T_3, T_5, \dots, T_{21}.$$
$$\text{Number of terms } n = 11.$$
$$\text{First term } a = 8, \quad \text{common ratio } r = \frac{32}{8} = 4.$$
$$S_{11} = \frac{a(r^{11} - 1)}{r - 1}$$
$$S_{11} = \frac{8(4^{11} - 1)}{4 - 1} = \frac{8(4\ 194\ 304 - 1)}{3} = \frac{8(4\ 194\ 303)}{3} = 11\ 184\ 808$$

$$\mathbf{OR/OF}$$

$$\text{Sum of all 21 terms} - \text{Sum of terms that are powers of } 4:$$
$$S_{21} = \frac{8(2^{21} - 1)}{2 - 1} = 8(2\ 097\ 151) = 16\ 777\ 208$$
$$\text{Powers of } 4: T_2, T_4, \dots, T_{20} \quad (10 \text{ terms}, a = 16, r = 4):$$
$$S_{10} = \frac{16(4^{10} - 1)}{4 - 1} = \frac{16(1\ 048\ 576 - 1)}{3} = 5\ 592\ 400$$
$$\text{Required sum} = 16\ 777\ 208 - 5\ 592\ 400 = 11\ 184\ 808$$

* $\checkmark n = 11$ (or $\frac{8(2^{21}-1)}{2-1}$)
* $\checkmark r = 4$ (or $n = 10$)
* $\checkmark \frac{8(4^{11} - 1)}{4 - 1}$ (or $\frac{16(4^{10}-1)}{4-1}$)
* $\checkmark 11\ 184\ 808$

question: Show that the general term of this sequence is $T_n = n^2 - 8n + 21$.

$$\text{First differences: } -5 \quad -3 \quad -1$$

$$a + b + c = 14 \implies 1 - 8 + c = 14 \implies c = 21$$
$$\therefore T_n = n^2 - 8n + 21$$

question: The graph of $g^{-1}$, the inverse of $g$, also passes through $B$. Determine the equation of $g$ in the form $y = \dots$
memo:
$$B(0\ ;\ -3) \text{ lies on } g^{-1} \implies E(-3\ ;\ 0) \text{ lies on } g.$$
$$\text{Points on } g: A(3\ ;\ 4) \text{ and } E(-3\ ;\ 0).$$
$$m = \frac{4 - 0}{3 - (-3)} = \frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3}$$
$$y - 0 = \frac{2}{3}(x - (-3))$$
$$y = \frac{2}{3}x + 2$$

$$\mathbf{OR/OF}$$

$$\text{For } g^{-1}: \text{ passes through } B(0\ ;\ -3) \text{ and } A'(4\ ;\ 3).$$
$$y = mx - 3$$
$$3 = m(4) - 3 \implies 4m = 6 \implies m = \frac{3}{2}$$
$$g^{-1}(x) = \frac{3}{2}x - 3$$
$$\text{For } g: \quad x = \frac{3}{2}y - 3$$
$$\frac{3}{2}y = x + 3$$
$$y = \frac{2}{3}x + 2$$

* $\checkmark E(-3\ ;\ 0)$

* $\checkmark$ substitution

question: Tino invests $\text{R}500\ 000$ in an account earning interest at the rate of $6\%\text{ p.a.}$, compounded quarterly. Tino decides to withdraw $\text{R}11\ 250$ at the end of every $3\text{ months}$. Tino will continue making these regular withdrawals until there is no money in the account. How many withdrawals of $\text{R}11\ 250$ will Tino be able to make?
memo:
$$P = \frac{x[1 - (1 + i)^{-n}]}{i}$$
$$i = \frac{0{,}06}{4} = 0{,}015$$
$$500\ 000 = \frac{11\ 250\left[1 - \left(1 + \frac{0{,}06}{4}\right)^{-n}\right]}{\frac{0{,}06}{4}}$$
$$\frac{500\ 000 \times 0{,}015}{11\ 250} = 1 - (1{,}015)^{-n}$$
$$\frac{7\ 500}{11\ 250} = \frac{2}{3} = 1 - (1{,}015)^{-n}$$
$$(1{,}015)^{-n} = 1 - \frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{3}$$
$$-n = \log_{1{,}015}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)$$
$$-n = -73{,}788\dots$$
$$n = 73{,}788\dots$$
$$\therefore \text{Number of full withdrawals of } \text{R}11\ 250 = 73\text{ withdrawals}$$

* $\checkmark i = \frac{0{,}06}{4}$
* $\checkmark$ substitution into correct formula
* $\checkmark$ correct use of logs
* $\checkmark$ answer for $n = 73{,}788\dots$
* $\checkmark$ final answer ($73\text{ withdrawals}$)

topic: Finance - Compound Interest and Future Value Annuity
question:
On **1 March 2021**, Abby made a once-off deposit of $\text{R}12\ 000$ into an account earning interest at a rate of $9{,}5\%\text{ p.a.}$, compounded monthly. She deposited $\text{R}500$ into the same account on **1 April 2023** and continues to make these monthly deposits of $\text{R}500$ on the first day of each month thereafter.

Calculate how much money was in the account immediately after the deposit of $\text{R}500$ is made on **1 March 2025**, exactly four full years after her initial deposit.
memo:
$$\text{Lump sum growth (1 March 2021 to 1 March 2025: } 4 \times 12 = 48 \text{ months):}$$
$$A = P(1 + i)^n = 12\ 000\left(1 + \frac{0{,}095}{12}\right)^{48} = \text{R}17\ 521{,}17895\dots$$

$$\text{Annuity payments (1 April 2023 to 1 March 2025: } 24 \text{ deposits):}$$
$$F = \frac{x[(1 + i)^n - 1]}{i} = \frac{500\left[\left(1 + \frac{0{,}095}{12}\right)^{24} - 1\right]}{\frac{0{,}095}{12}} = \text{R}13\ 158{,}64744\dots$$

$$\text{Total in account} = 17\ 521{,}17895\dots + 13\ 158{,}64744\dots = \text{R}30\ 679{,}83$$

* $\checkmark i = \frac{0{,}095}{12}$
* $\checkmark n = 48$ in $A$
* $\checkmark$ substitution into compound formula
* $\checkmark n = 24$ in $F$
* $\checkmark$ substitution into future value formula
* $\checkmark$ adding compound and future values ($\text{R}30\ 679{,}83$)

question: Determine $f'(x)$ from first principles if it is given that $f(x) = x^2 - 2$
memo:
$$f(x) = x^2 - 2$$
$$f(x + h) = (x + h)^2 - 2 = x^2 + 2xh + h^2 - 2$$
$$f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}$$
$$f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(x^2 + 2xh + h^2 - 2) - (x^2 - 2)}{h}$$
$$f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{2xh + h^2}{h}$$
$$f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{h(2x + h)}{h}$$
$$f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0}(2x + h)$$
$$f'(x) = 2x$$

$$\mathbf{OR/OF}$$

$$f(x+h) - f(x) = (x+h)^2 - 2 - (x^2 - 2) = 2xh + h^2$$
$$f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{h(2x+h)}{h} = 2x$$

* $\checkmark f(x+h) = x^2 + 2xh + h^2 - 2$
* $\checkmark$ substitution into formula
* $\checkmark$ simplification ($2xh + h^2$)
* $\checkmark$ factorisation ($h(2x + h)$)
* $\checkmark$ answer ($2x$)

question: Given that $y = 4x - 14$ is a common tangent to $f(x) = 2x^2 - 4x - 6$ and $g(x) = ax^2 + bx - 18$, calculate the values of $a$ and $b$.
memo:
$$\text{Tangent line: } y = 4x - 14 \implies m = 4$$
$$f'(x) = 4x - 4$$
$$4x - 4 = 4 \implies 4x = 8 \implies x = 2$$
$$y = 4(2) - 14 = -6$$
$$\text{Point of contact on } f \text{ is } (2\ ;\ -6).$$

$$\text{Since } y = 4x - 14 \text{ is also tangent to } g(x) \text{ at } (2\ ;\ -6):$$
$$g(2) = a(2)^2 + b(2) - 18 = -6$$
$$4a + 2b - 18 = -6$$
$$4a + 2b = 12 \quad \dots (1)$$

$$g'(x) = 2ax + b$$
$$g'(2) = 2a(2) + b = 4$$
$$4a + b = 4 \quad \dots (2)$$

$$\text{Subtract (2) from (1):}$$
$$(4a + 2b) - (4a + b) = 12 - 4$$
$$b = 8$$

$$\text{Substitute } b = 8 \text{ into (2):}$$
$$4a + 8 = 4$$
$$4a = -4$$
$$a = -1$$

$$\mathbf{OR/OF}$$

$$2x^2 - 4x - 6 = 4x - 14$$
$$2x^2 - 8x + 8 = 0$$
$$x^2 - 4x + 4 = 0$$
$$(x - 2)^2 = 0 \implies x = 2$$
$$y = 4(2) - 14 = -6 \implies (2\ ;\ -6)$$
$$g(2) = -6 \implies 4a + 2b = 12 \quad \dots (1)$$
$$g'(2) = 4 \implies 4a + b = 4 \quad \dots (2)$$
$$b = 8, \quad a = -1$$

* $\checkmark 4x - 4$
* $\checkmark = 4$
* $\checkmark y = -6$
* $\checkmark g(2) = -6 \implies 4a + 2b = 12$
* $\checkmark g'(2) = 4 \implies 4a + b = 4$
* $\checkmark a = -1, \quad b = 8$

question: Calculate the maximum vertical distance between $f$ and $h$ for $1 < x < 3$, if $h(x) = -2f'(x)$.
memo:
$$f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 9$$
$$h(x) = -2f'(x) = -2(3x^2 - 12x + 9) = -6x^2 + 24x - 18$$
$$\text{For } 1 < x < 3, \quad h(x) > f(x).$$
$$\text{Distance } d(x) = h(x) - f(x)$$
$$d(x) = (-6x^2 + 24x - 18) - (x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x - 4)$$
$$d(x) = -6x^2 + 24x - 18 - x^3 + 6x^2 - 9x + 4$$
$$d(x) = -x^3 + 15x - 14$$

$$\text{For maximum distance, } d'(x) = 0:$$
$$d'(x) = -3x^2 + 15 = 0$$
$$3x^2 = 15$$
$$x^2 = 5$$
$$x = \pm\sqrt{5}$$
$$\text{Since } 1 < x < 3: \quad x = \sqrt{5} \approx 2{,}24$$

$$\text{Maximum distance } = d(\sqrt{5}):$$
$$d(\sqrt{5}) = -(\sqrt{5})^3 + 15(\sqrt{5}) - 14 = -5\sqrt{5} + 15\sqrt{5} - 14 = 10\sqrt{5} - 14 \approx 8{,}36$$

* $\checkmark h(x) = -2f'(x) = -6x^2 + 24x - 18$
* $\checkmark$ simplification ($d(x) = -x^3 + 15x - 14$)
* $\checkmark$ first derivative ($-3x^2 + 15$)
* $\checkmark = 0$
* $\checkmark x\text{-value } (x = \sqrt{5})$
* $\checkmark$ answer ($8{,}36$)

question:
A game at a fun park requires a player to roll a six-sided dice and pick a card from a deck of 52 cards.

A player wins if an odd number appears on the uppermost face of the dice and the player also draws a picture card from the deck.

* A deck of cards has 4 suites (hearts, diamonds, spades and clubs).
* There are 4 picture cards (king, queen, jack and ace) in every suite.

A player pays $\text{R}10$ to play a game and in an hour, 260 people can each play one game. If the owner wants to make a $70\%$ profit per hour, calculate the maximum amount that the owner must pay out to each winner.
memo:
$$\text{Total money collected per hour} = 260 \times \text{R}10 = \text{R}2\ 600$$
$$\text{Profit desired} = 70\% \times \text{R}2\ 600 = 0{,}7 \times \text{R}2\ 600 = \text{R}1\ 820$$
$$\text{Total value of pay-outs} = \text{R}2\ 600 - \text{R}1\ 820 = \text{R}780 \quad \text{OR/OF} \quad 0{,}3 \times \text{R}2\ 600 = \text{R}780$$

$$P(\text{winning}) = P(\text{odd on dice}) \times P(\text{picture card})$$
$$P(\text{winning}) = \frac{3}{6} \times \frac{16}{52} = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{4}{13} = \frac{2}{13}$$

$$\text{Expected number of winners} = \frac{2}{13} \times 260 = 40\text{ winners}$$
$$\text{Pay-out per winner} = \frac{\text{R}780}{40} = \text{R}19{,}50$$

* $\checkmark \text{R}1\ 820$ (or $0{,}3 \times \text{R}2\ 600$)
* $\checkmark$ amount willing to pay out ($\text{R}780$)
* $\checkmark \frac{16}{52}$
* $\checkmark \frac{2}{13}$
* $\checkmark$ winners ($40$)
* $\checkmark$ pay-out ($\text{R}19{,}50$)

passage: Consider the three-digit numbers from $501$ up to $999$.
question: How many of these three-digit numbers have exactly one $5$ in them?
memo:
$$\text{Case 1: The } 5 \text{ is in the hundreds digit:}$$
$$\text{Hundreds digit: } 5 \quad (1 \text{ choice})$$
$$\text{Tens digit: any digit except } 5 \quad (9 \text{ choices: } 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9)$$
$$\text{Units digit: any digit except } 5 \quad (9 \text{ choices})$$
$$1 \times 9 \times 9 = 81$$
$$\text{Since } 500 \text{ is not included in the range } (501 \text{ to } 999):$$
$$81 - 1 = 80 \text{ possibilities}$$

$$\text{Case 2: The } 5 \text{ is in the tens digit:}$$
$$\text{Hundreds digit: } 6, 7, 8, 9 \quad (4 \text{ choices})$$
$$\text{Tens digit: } 5 \quad (1 \text{ choice})$$
$$\text{Units digit: any digit except } 5 \quad (9 \text{ choices})$$
$$4 \times 1 \times 9 = 36 \text{ possibilities}$$

$$\text{Case 3: The } 5 \text{ is in the units digit:}$$
$$\text{Hundreds digit: } 6, 7, 8, 9 \quad (4 \text{ choices})$$
$$\text{Tens digit: any digit except } 5 \quad (9 \text{ choices})$$
$$\text{Units digit: } 5 \quad (1 \text{ choice})$$
$$4 \times 9 \times 1 = 36 \text{ possibilities}$$

$$\text{Total possibilities} = 80 + 36 + 36 = 152$$

$$\mathbf{OR/OF}$$

$$501 \text{ to } 599: \quad 99 - 10 - 9 = 80 \text{ possibilities}$$
$$601 \text{ to } 699: \quad 9 + 9 = 18 \text{ possibilities of having a } 5 \text{ in the tens or units digit.}$$
$$\text{Thus } 600 \text{ to } 999 = 4 \times 18 = 72 \text{ possibilities.}$$
$$\text{Total possibilities} = 80 + 4 \times 18 = 152$$

* $\checkmark 1 \times 9 \times 9$ (or 80)
* $\checkmark 4 \times 1 \times 9$ (or 18)
* $\checkmark 4 \times 9 \times 1$ (or $4 \times 18$)
* $\checkmark 152$

memo:

$$n(S) = 999 - 501 + 1 = 499$$

$$P(\text{not having exactly one } 5) = 1 - P(\text{having exactly one } 5)$$

* $\checkmark 1 - P(\text{having number})$
